blocks.sub: Benchmarked partitions, reproducible ensembles and estate economics

blocks.x: HPC is where this domain pays the bills today: risk Monte Carlo, CFD/FEA, molecular dynamics, large-scale optimization. The engineering is workload-shaped, solvers tuned to the math, clusters benchmarked like engines (HPL and application-level), data pipelines that feed simulations with provenance, and a cost-per-solve metric that keeps the queue honest.

The practice covers architecture (CPU/GPU mix by workload), the solver library with versioned performance, workflow orchestration for ensembles, and the utilization discipline that separates an HPC asset from an HPC bill.

widgets.title: Parallel efficiency vs rank count — the Amdahl ceiling in the data
widgets.note: Click to isolate. The serial-cap line is Amdahl's law made visible: at 9% serial fraction, 4,096 ranks can never exceed 31% efficiency — which is why the solver change preceded the cluster order.

widgets.title: Speedup what-if — serial fraction, comm overhead, precision
widgets.note: The speedup curve collapses as serial fraction grows — at 30%, a thousand ranks buy nothing. Drag precision gain against it: mixed precision is often the cheapest speedup on the panel.

nodes.label: Physics kernels
nodes.detail: Governing equations discretized per domain (CFD, FEA, electromagnetics) with the discretization error budget declared per study.

nodes.label: Mesh strategy
nodes.detail: Adaptive refinement where the error concentrates — refinement driven by error estimators, not by habit.

nodes.label: Linear solvers
nodes.detail: Krylov with preconditioning (multigrid where the operator allows) — convergence monitored, divergence handled by fallback chains.

nodes.label: Precision plan
nodes.detail: Mixed precision where numerics tolerate: 1.5–2× on GPUs for free, with stability watched by the regression suite.

nodes.label: Cluster scheduling
nodes.detail: Jobs scheduled against license and power constraints with backfill — the queue is engineered, not suffered.

nodes.label: Known-answer tests
nodes.detail: Analytical cases per solver configuration — every solver change passes KAT before production studies.

nodes.label: Regression suite
nodes.detail: Convergence-rate checks on canonical problems — solver drift is caught numerically, not by a physicist's frown.

widgets.note: Click nodes for the verification contract each layer carries. The KAT lane is what makes speedups publishable — a fast wrong answer is worse than a slow right one.

Cost per solve is the headline
blocks.sub: Benchmarked partitions, reproducible ensembles and the estate economics that fund science

blocks.x: HPC estates rot through folklore: partitions tuned by habit, solvers upgraded on vendor calendars, ensembles nobody can reproduce. The engineering disciplines them, partitions benchmarked per workload class with application benchmarks (not linpack alone), a solver library that is versioned and pinned with upgrade evidence, and ensemble orchestration that is seeded and reproducible: the same inputs produce the same ensemble, on demand, which is what makes simulation results citable.

Cost per solve is the headline metric because it is the number that funds the estate: per-solve cost trended by class, allocation decisions argued from it, and queue policies designed against it (a job that starves the partition for a weekend is a scheduling decision, not a right). The reproducibility overlay keeps the science honest, seeds archived, environments versioned, and the benchmark suite pinned so results compare across years rather than across press releases.

items: Per-class benchmarks that reflect the workloads actually run.
Versioned with upgrade evidence; folklore replaced by record.
Seeded, archived, re-runnable, results stay citable.
The number that drives allocation and queue policy.

Folklore tuning, unbenchmarked upgrades and scheduler drift: each change feels justified, none is measured. The estate is benchmarked per workload class, so a build earns its numbers, 80→94 on risk workloads, before users inherit it.
Fixed benchmark suites per workload class, risk, CFD, ensembles, run on every candidate configuration, with variance reported. A score without variance is a rumor; the gates read the distribution.
Can you work with our existing cluster?
Yes, the benchmarked estate overlays what exists: schedulers and storage enter through the integration surface, and the first build is a measurement pass that prices what tuning would buy.
The overlay versions solvers, inputs and environment per result; ensembles carry seeds and manifests so a verified result re-runs bit-for-bit. The reproducibility drill is a release gate.
The benchmarked platform, the console with cost per solve as the headline, the gates and the reproducibility overlay, the team runs compute as an engineering asset, not a utility bill.
